title: Part 2, Chapter 34
paragraphs: Which relates how they learned the method by which the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso was to be disenchanted — one of the most remarkable adventures in this book

The duke and duchess took enormous delight in the conversation of Don Quixote and Sancho Panza, and, more determined than ever to carry out their scheme of playing tricks on the pair that would carry the look and feel of real adventures, they took as their starting point what Don Quixote had already told them about the cave of Montesinos, planning to stage a famous prank on that basis. What astonished the duchess above everything else, though, was that Sancho could be simple enough to accept as gospel truth that Dulcinea had been enchanted, when he himself had been the enchanter and the trickster behind the whole affair. So, having briefed their servants on everything they were to do, six days later they took Don Quixote out hunting, with a retinue of huntsmen and beaters worthy of a crowned king.

They offered Don Quixote a hunting outfit, and Sancho another of the finest green cloth; but Don Quixote refused to put his on, saying that he would soon have to return to the harsh calling of arms and could not travel with wardrobes or baggage. Sancho, on the other hand, accepted what they gave him, intending to sell it at the first chance he got.

When the appointed day came, Don Quixote put on his armor and Sancho dressed himself up, and mounted on his Dapple — for he refused to give the donkey up even though they offered him a horse — he took his place among the crowd of huntsmen. The duchess rode out magnificently dressed, and Don Quixote, out of pure courtesy and good manners, held the rein of her palfrey, although the duke tried to prevent it; and at last they reached a wood lying between two high mountains, where, after taking up various stations, ambush points, and paths, and posting the party in different positions, the hunt opened with a great racket of shouting and hallooing, so that between the baying of the hounds and the blare of the horns nobody could hear anyone else. The duchess dismounted and, with a sharp boar-spear in her hand, stationed herself at a spot where she knew the wild boars usually passed. The duke and Don Quixote dismounted as well and placed themselves on either side of her. Sancho posted himself behind everyone without getting off Dapple, whom he did not dare abandon for fear some harm might come to him. They had hardly formed their line with a number of their servants when they saw a huge boar bearing down on them, hard pressed by the hounds and pursued by the huntsmen, gnashing his teeth and tusks and flinging foam from his mouth. The moment Don Quixote saw him, he braced his shield on his arm, drew his sword, and stepped forward to meet him; the duke did the same with his boar-spear; and the duchess would have gone out in front of them all if the duke had not stopped her. Only Sancho, deserting Dapple at the sight of the formidable beast, ran for it as fast as his legs would carry him and tried in vain to climb a tall oak. While he was clinging to a branch halfway up, struggling toward the top, the bough — such was his bad luck and hard fate — snapped, and as he fell he was caught on a broken stub of the oak and left hanging in midair, unable to reach the ground. Finding himself in this fix, noticing that the green coat was beginning to tear, and reflecting that if the savage animal came that way it might be able to reach him, he began to let out such yells and to cry for help so desperately that everyone who heard him without seeing him was convinced he must be in the jaws of some wild beast. In the end the tusked boar went down, run through by the blades of the many spears leveled against him; and Don Quixote, turning at the sound of Sancho's cries — for he recognized them at once as his — saw him dangling head downward from the oak, with Dapple, who had not abandoned him in his trouble, standing close by; and Cide Hamete remarks that he rarely saw Sancho Panza without seeing Dapple, or Dapple without seeing Sancho Panza, so deep was the attachment and loyalty between the two. Don Quixote went over and unhooked Sancho, who, the moment he found himself on solid ground, examined the tear in his hunting coat and was grieved to the bottom of his heart, for he had thought of that suit as a family estate.

Meanwhile the others had slung the mighty boar across a mule's back, covered it with sprigs of rosemary and branches of myrtle, and carried it off as a trophy of victory to some large field tents that had been pitched in the middle of the wood, where they found the tables set and dinner laid out in a style so grand and lavish that it was easy to gauge the rank and wealth of their hosts. Sancho, showing the duchess the rips in his torn suit, remarked, “If we had been hunting hares, or going after little birds, my coat would have been spared the state it's in now; I don't see what pleasure there can be in lying in wait for an animal that can take your life with a tusk if it reaches you. I remember hearing an old ballad sung that goes,

May you be eaten by bears, as once
Was the famous Favila.”
“That,” said Don Quixote, “was a Gothic king who went out hunting and was devoured by a bear.”

“Exactly,” said Sancho; “and I wouldn't want kings and princes putting themselves in dangers like that for the sake of a pleasure which, to my way of thinking, shouldn't be one at all, since it amounts to killing an animal that has done no harm whatsoever.”

“On the contrary, Sancho, there you are mistaken,” said the duke; “for hunting is more fitting and more necessary for kings and princes than for anyone else. The chase is an image of war: it has its stratagems, its tricks, and its cunning devices for defeating the enemy without risk; in it one must endure bitter cold and unbearable heat; idleness and sleep are held in contempt; the body's strength is built up and the limbs of whoever practices it are made agile; in short, it is a pursuit that can be followed without injuring anyone and with enjoyment for many; and the best part of it is that it is not open to everybody, as other kinds of field sport are — except hawking, which is likewise reserved for kings and great lords. So change your opinion, Sancho, and when you are a governor take up hunting, and you will find it does you good.”

“Not a chance,” said Sancho; “a good governor should be like a man with a broken leg — stay at home;” it would be a fine thing if people went to the trouble of coming to see him on business only to find the governor off in the forest amusing himself; the government would go to ruin that way. Honestly, señor, hunting and entertainments are better suited to idlers than to governors; what I plan to amuse myself with is a game of all fours at Eastertime, and bowls on Sundays and holidays; all this hunting doesn't fit my station or sit well with my conscience.”
“God grant it works out that way,” said the duke, “because there's a long stretch between saying and doing.”

“Be that as it may,” said Sancho, “‘a good payer isn't troubled by pledges,’ and ‘the man God helps does better than the man who rises early,’ and ‘it's the belly that carries the feet, not the feet the belly;’ what I mean is that if God gives me his help and I do my duty honestly, I'll certainly govern better than a gerfalcon. Just let them put a finger in my mouth, and they'll find out whether I can bite or not.”

“The curse of God and all his saints on you, wretched Sancho!” exclaimed Don Quixote. “When will the day come — as I have told you so many times — when I hear you produce a single coherent, sensible remark without proverbs? Your highnesses, I beg you, leave this fool alone, for he will grind your souls between not two but two thousand proverbs, hauled in as timely and as much to the point as — may God give him good health for it, or me, if I'm willing to listen to them!”

“Sancho Panza's proverbs,” said the duchess, “though more numerous than the Greek Commander's, are not to be valued any less for the pithiness of their maxims. Speaking for myself, I can say they give me more pleasure than others that may be more aptly chosen and brought in at a better moment.”

Talking pleasantly in this fashion they left the tent and went into the wood, and the day passed in visiting some of the stations and hiding places, until night came on — not, however, as clear or as calm as might have been expected for the season, since it was then midsummer, but bringing with it a kind of haze that served the duke and duchess's plot very well. So as night was falling, a little after twilight set in, the whole wood suddenly seemed to blaze up on all four sides, and shortly afterward, here, there, and everywhere, an enormous number of trumpets and other instruments of war were heard, as though several troops of cavalry were riding through the wood. The glare of the fires and the noise of the martial instruments all but blinded the eyes and deafened the ears of those standing there, and indeed of everyone in the wood. Then came repeated lelilies, the war cries the Moors raise when they charge into battle; trumpets and clarions blared, drums pounded, fifes shrilled, so continuously and so fast that no one could have kept his senses amid the confused din of so many instruments. The duke was thunderstruck, the duchess amazed, Don Quixote full of wonder, Sancho Panza shaking — and even those in on the secret were frightened. Fear silenced them all, and a postilion got up as a demon rode past in front of them, blowing, instead of a bugle, a huge hollow horn that gave out a hideous, rasping note.
“Ho there, brother courier!” called the duke. “Who are you? Where are you bound? What troops are these that seem to be passing through the wood?”

To which the courier answered in a harsh, grating voice, “I am the devil; I am looking for Don Quixote of La Mancha; the company coming this way is six troops of enchanters, bringing the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso on a triumphal car; she comes under enchantment, together with the gallant Frenchman Montesinos, to instruct Don Quixote in how she, the said lady, may be freed from her enchantment.”

“If you really were the devil, as you claim and as your appearance suggests,” said the duke, “you would have recognized the said knight, Don Quixote of La Mancha, for he is standing here in front of you.”
“By God and on my conscience,” said the devil, “I never noticed him, for my mind is taken up with so many different matters that I was forgetting the chief business I came about.”

“This demon must be an honest fellow and a good Christian,” said Sancho; “otherwise he wouldn't swear by God and his conscience. I'm convinced now that there must be decent souls even down in hell itself.”

Then, without dismounting, the demon turned to Don Quixote and said, “The unfortunate but valiant knight Montesinos sends me to you, Knight of the Lions — and would that I saw you in their claws — charging me to tell you to wait for him wherever I find you, since he brings with him the lady they call Dulcinea del Toboso, so that he may show you what must be done to free her from her enchantment; and since I came for nothing more, I need stay no longer; may demons of my kind be with you, and good angels with these gentlefolk.” And with that he blew his enormous horn, wheeled around, and rode off without waiting for an answer from anyone.

Fresh astonishment seized them all, but especially Sancho and Don Quixote — Sancho at seeing how, in flat defiance of the truth, everyone insisted that Dulcinea was enchanted; Don Quixote because he still could not be certain whether what had happened to him in the cave of Montesinos was real or not; and while he was sunk in these reflections the duke asked him, “Do you intend to wait, Señor Don Quixote?”
“Why not?” he replied. “Here I will wait, fearless and steadfast, though all hell itself should come to attack me.”
“Well, if I see another devil or hear another horn like that last one, I'll wait here about as readily as I'd wait in Flanders,” said Sancho.

Night had now fully closed in, and many lights began to dart about through the wood, just as the fiery vapors rising from the earth — which look to our eyes like shooting stars — streak across the sky; and at the same time a dreadful noise was heard, like the sound made by the solid wheels of ox-carts, whose harsh, unceasing creaking is said to drive off bears and wolves, if there are any along the route. On top of all this commotion came a further disturbance to swell the uproar, for now it truly seemed as though four skirmishes or battles were being fought at once on all four sides of the wood: in one quarter rumbled the dull thunder of a fearsome cannonade, in another countless muskets were being fired, the shouts of the combatants sounded almost at hand, and farther off the Moorish lelilies rose again and again. In short, the bugles, the horns, the clarions, the trumpets, the drums, the cannon, the musket fire, and above everything the tremendous racket of the carts, together made up a din so confused and so terrifying that Don Quixote had to summon all his courage to face it; but Sancho's failed him altogether, and he collapsed in a faint onto the skirt of the duchess's gown. She let him lie there and promptly ordered water to be thrown in his face. This was done, and he had come around by the time one of the creaking-wheeled carts reached the spot. It was drawn by four plodding oxen all draped in black coverings; to each horn was fastened a large lighted wax taper, and on top of the cart was built a raised seat on which sat a venerable old man with a beard whiter than snow itself, and so long that it hung below his waist; he wore a long robe of black buckram, and since the cart bristled with a multitude of candles, everything on it could be seen plainly. Leading it were two hideous demons, likewise dressed in buckram, with faces so frightful that Sancho, having looked at them once, shut his eyes so as not to see them again. When the cart drew level with the spot, the old man rose from his lofty seat, stood, and declared in a loud voice, “I am the sage Lirgandeo,” and without another word the cart rolled on. Behind it came another of the same design, carrying another aged man enthroned, who halted the cart and announced in a voice no less solemn than the first's, “I am the sage Alquife, great friend of Urganda the Unknown,” and passed on. Then a third cart came by at the same pace, but the figure on the throne was not old like the others; he was a big, powerfully built man with a menacing face, who as he came up proclaimed in a voice far hoarser and more devilish, “I am the enchanter Archelaus, mortal enemy of Amadis of Gaul and all his kin,” and then passed on. A short distance farther on the three carts halted and the grinding noise of their wheels stopped, and soon afterward they heard something else — not noise this time, but the sound of sweet, harmonious music, which delighted Sancho, who took it for a good omen; and he said to the duchess, from whose side he would not stir a step or for a single instant, “Señora, where there's music there can't be any mischief.”

“Nor where there are lights and brightness,” said the duchess; to which Sancho answered, “Fire gives light, and it's bright around bonfires, as we can see from the ones surrounding us right now — which may well burn us yet; but music is a sign of feasting and merrymaking.”
“That remains to be seen,” said Don Quixote, who had been listening to all of it; and he was right, as the following chapter shows.
